title: Ireland's 2025 PISA Reading Results: “Ah, We're Not That Great, Really.”
author: Jen
summary: Using Ireland's cultural discomfort with compliments as a framing device, this piece analyzes Ireland's 2025 PISA reading results with a deliberately measured tone. The author notes the genuinely strong headline results — first in the EU, seventh in the world, well above the OECD average — while insisting these are read against a real 16-point decline since 2022 that deserves urgent attention rather than dismissal. She argues that Ireland's two habitual reactions to PISA data, reflexive self-congratulation or reflexive self-flagellation, are both unhelpful, and that the more useful response lies between them. A key point is that strong national averages mask significant internal inequity: pupils in DEIS (socioeconomically disadvantaged) schools underperform their peers by 49 points, meaning international ranking says little about whether every child is thriving. She calls for identifying the 'protective factors' — oral language tradition, curriculum, teacher adaptability — that may be cushioning Ireland from the sharper declines seen elsewhere, while watching for signs those factors are weakening, including a new curricular framework that reduces dedicated literacy instruction time. The essay closes by urging a 'cautious celebration': genuine credit to teachers and students, paired with sustained attention to the downward trend and the children hidden within the averages.

quotes: We ranked first in the European Union, 7th in the world, and remain significantly above the OECD average.
This is where rankings can seem more flattering than they actually are. While comparatively our scores internationally are very strong, like many other countries, our reading levels are declining.
We have dropped 16 points since 2022 and are experiencing a downward trajectory that needs some serious and urgent attention.

We quickly see that children attending DEIS schools (schools situated in more socioeconomically deprived areas) are underperforming significantly in comparison to their peers in non-DEIS schools. To the tune of 49 points.

Ireland remains one of the strongest-performing education systems in the world for reading. That is something to value and celebrate. At the same time, the downward trajectory is real and deserves our attention, especially in light of a new curricular framework which sees dedicated time for literacy instruction being reduced.
We can celebrate our international standing while remaining concerned about the children hidden within the averages.
Ireland’s literacy system is not broken. It needs some urgent attention but, for most children, it’s doing what it says on the tin.
